chunks: And as for that which was narrated - Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Ayub ibn Nuh from Hariz from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

‘Nursing does not cause prohibition except what is compulsory.’ I said, ‘And what is the compulsory?’ He said, ‘A mother who raises [the child], or a mother who raises, or a wet-nurse who is hired, or a servant who is purchased, or something similar that is contingent upon it.’ Therefore, this narration does not contradict what we have previously presented from the narrations regarding the prohibition of nursing, because the intent of this narration is to negate the prohibition regarding one who nurses for a single suck or two sucks or something similar to that. As for when the woman nurses the amount that we have mentioned regarding the prohibition, even if it is not with these characteristics, then it causes prohibition in any case. And that which indicates what we have presented is what was narrated:

key_terms.أُمٌّ مُرَبِّيَةٌ: A mother who raises the child

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between compulsory and voluntary breastfeeding in Shia jurisprudence regarding marital prohibition?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi utilizes this narration from Al-Fadl ibn Yasar to resolve apparent contradictions in the jurisprudence of *radha'* (breastfeeding), clarifying that the prohibition applies to the specific quantity of milk consumed rather than the social status of the nurse. This distinction ensures that casual nursing does not create *mahramiyyah*, while sufficient nursing does, regardless of whether the nurse is a mother, hired wet-nurse, or servant. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise quantification (*kamm*) over qualitative circumstances in establishing kinship ties.
